blurb: The physical side of AI: buildings full of hot chips, how they're cooled, how much electricity they use, and the race to build more.

steps.p: A data center is a warehouse of tall metal cabinets (racks), each packed with servers. AI racks are crammed with GPUs.
A traditional server rack might draw 5–15 kilowatts. The newest AI racks draw over 100 — ten times more, like dozens of homes in one cabinet.
Nearly every watt a chip uses turns into heat, which must be removed or the chips throttle and fail. Cooling is half the engineering.
steps.analogy: Running thousands of hair dryers in a room and trying to keep it at room temperature.

steps.p: PUE compares total building power with the power the computers themselves use. 1.0 would be perfect; good modern sites reach about 1.1.
Thousands of GPUs must swap data constantly, so AI data centers have extremely fast internal networks, often fibre-optic.

options: About 10% extra power goes to cooling and other overhead
cards.why: 10% overhead. For every 100 units the computers use, the building draws 110 in total. Older sites were often around 1.5–2.

cards.q: Roughly how much more power does a modern AI rack draw than a traditional server rack?
cards.why: Ten times or more. That density is why old data centers often can't host the newest AI hardware without major rebuilding.

cards.statement: Liquid cooling is becoming standard for the newest, densest AI racks.
cards.why: True. Air simply can't carry heat away fast enough at 100+ kilowatts per rack. Cold liquid is piped right to the chips.

cards.title: xAI said it built its "Colossus" supercomputer in Memphis with 100,000 GPUs in 122 days.
cards.detail: Such projects usually take years. To get power fast, the site initially used on-site gas turbines, which drew local environmental complaints.

cards.statement: Where AI data centers are built is driven mainly by cheap land.
cards.why: False. Access to large amounts of electricity — and how quickly the grid can connect you — matters far more.

cards.title: How much power does AI really use?

steps.p: In 2024 all data centers together used about 1.5% of the world's electricity, by the International Energy Agency's estimate. AI is a growing part of that.
The IEA projected data-center electricity use could roughly double by 2030, with AI the main driver.
Small globally, but intense locally: in Ireland, data centers use around a fifth of the country's electricity.
Training a big model uses a lot at once. But serving millions of users every day adds up to more over the model's lifetime.
A typical chatbot question uses roughly a few tenths of a watt-hour — like running a light bulb for a few minutes, not boiling a kettle.
steps.analogy: One drop is nothing; billions of drops a day fill a reservoir.

cards.q: According to the IEA, what share of world electricity did data centers use in 2024?
cards.why: About 1.5%. Small overall, but growing fast and concentrated in a few regions, which strains local grids.

cards.statement: A typical chatbot question uses about as much energy as boiling a kettle.
cards.why: False. Recent estimates for a typical text query are a fraction of a watt-hour; a kettle uses around 100. Long reasoning or video generation can cost far more.

cards.q: For a widely used model, which usually uses more energy over its lifetime?
cards.why: Everyday use. Training is a one-off. Millions of people asking questions every day for months adds up to more.

cards.title: Microsoft agreed to buy power from a restarted reactor at Three Mile Island for its data centers.
cards.detail: The 2024 deal covers Unit 1 — not the reactor damaged in 1979 — which shut down in 2019 for economic reasons. It was renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center.

cards.statement: Major tech companies have signed deals to buy power from small modular nuclear reactors.
cards.why: True. Google, Amazon and others signed agreements in 2024 for future small reactors, seeking steady carbon-free power around the clock.

steps.p: Many data centers cool by letting water evaporate, which carries heat away — the same way sweat cools you. The evaporated water is gone.
steps.analogy: A data center sweating to stay cool.

steps.p: Others circulate water or coolant in sealed pipes and dump heat through big radiators. Little water is lost, but more electricity is used.
Water carries thousands of times more heat per litre than air, which is why liquid cooling handles dense AI racks.
Power stations also use water for cooling. So the electricity a data center buys has a water footprint too.
Some sites, especially in Nordic countries, pipe their waste heat into district heating networks that warm nearby homes.

cards.q: Why do evaporative cooling systems use up water rather than just moving it around?
options: Heat is removed by evaporating water, which leaves as vapour
The water leaks into the ground
cards.why: Evaporation takes the water. Turning water into vapour absorbs lots of heat — that's the cooling — and the vapour drifts away.

cards.statement: All of a data center's water footprint comes from its own cooling.
cards.why: False. Power stations generating its electricity often use water too. Full estimates include both.

cards.q: Liquid cooling works so much better than air mainly because water…
options: Carries thousands of times more heat per litre
cards.why: Heat capacity. A litre of water soaks up vastly more heat than a litre of air before warming up.

cards.title: Microsoft once ran a sealed data center on the seabed off Scotland's Orkney Islands.
cards.detail: Project Natick's two-year experiment, ending in 2020, found servers failed at one-eighth the rate of a land-based comparison group — possibly thanks to the nitrogen atmosphere and no human handling.

cards.q: Some Nordic data centers cut waste by…
options: Piping waste heat into district heating for homes
Using only solar panels on the roof
cards.why: Heating homes. The heat would otherwise be thrown away. Cold climates and existing heat networks make it practical.

steps.p: The biggest planned AI sites need a gigawatt or more — about the output of a large nuclear reactor, enough for hundreds of thousands of homes.
Connecting a huge new power user to the grid can take years of studies and upgrades. Sometimes the chips are ready long before the power is.
Big tech companies are each spending tens of billions of dollars a year on AI infrastructure. Stargate (2025) pledged up to $500 billion.
Power ≈ number of GPUs × about 1 kilowatt each (including cooling and networking). 100,000 GPUs ≈ 100 megawatts.
steps.analogy: Like estimating a party's food by "people × one plate".

steps.p: Spending at this scale is a bet that AI demand keeps growing fast. If it doesn't, some of it may prove too much.

cards.statement: One gigawatt of data-center capacity draws roughly the output of a large nuclear reactor.
cards.why: True. A big reactor produces about 1 GW. A single AI campus may now need that much power on its own.

cards.q: Why do grid connection queues matter so much for AI data centers?
options: Connecting a big new power user can take years, delaying projects even when chips are ready
They decide what the AI can say
cards.why: Power is the bottleneck. Building a data center takes about two years; upgrading the grid can take longer.

cards.q: Using about 1 kilowatt per GPU, how much power does a 100,000-GPU cluster need?
cards.why: About 100 MW. 100,000 kilowatts = 100 megawatts — roughly a small city's demand.

cards.title: Big tech's spending on AI rivals the largest infrastructure programmes in history.
cards.detail: Annual spending of hundreds of billions of dollars exceeds what most countries spend on all their roads and railways, raising questions about whether demand will justify it.

cards.title: Estimate a cluster's power
cards.body: When you hear "X GPUs", multiply by about 1 kilowatt for a rough total including cooling. It makes headlines easier to judge.
cards.challenge: Next time you read about a new AI supercomputer, estimate its power and compare it with a town's demand.
